name: CBT for BDD
lead: Cognitive-behavioral therapy for body dysmorphic disorder (CBT-BDD) is a form of psychotherapy designed for people with body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a condition marked by preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance. Treatment typically combines psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, exposure with response prevention (ERP), and in some programs mindfulness and perceptual retraining.[1][2]

It is described in the research literature as the best-studied psychological treatment for BDD.[3] A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials examined its effect on validated BDD measures,[4] and a 2019 randomized trial compared therapist-delivered CBT with supportive psychotherapy.[5] Researchers have also tested app-based and digital versions and adolescent programs.[6][7][8]

In looksmaxxing communities, BDD is discussed as a condition that can overlap with appearance-focused self-improvement, and therapy is sometimes raised as an alternative or complement to cosmetic procedures. Wikipedia notes that many people with BDD seek cosmetic or dermatologic treatment that typically does not relieve their distress.[1]

paras: BDD is classified in the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders group in the DSM-5.[1] People with BDD spend substantial time thinking about a perceived defect and often perform repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking, reassurance seeking, comparing and camouflaging.[1]

A modular CBT program described by Wilhelm and colleagues includes psychoeducation and case formulation, cognitive restructuring, exposure and ritual (response) prevention, and mindfulness and perceptual retraining, according to Wikipedia's summary.[1] In ERP, a person gradually faces feared appearance-related situations, such as going without camouflage, while refraining from the usual checking or avoidance rituals.[3]

A coach-supported smartphone app called Perspectives covers psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, exposure with response prevention, mindfulness, attention retraining and relapse prevention, and was tested in an initial randomized waitlist-controlled trial.[6] An earlier pilot tested a digital CBT service for BDD.[9]
Adolescent-specific CBT has been examined in a case series and in a follow-up of a randomized trial.[7][10]

A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of CBT for BDD, covering published and unpublished trials to November 2015, used validated BDD measures as primary outcomes and depression and insight as secondary outcomes.[4]

A randomized clinical trial published in JAMA Psychiatry in 2019 compared therapist-delivered CBT-BDD with supportive psychotherapy in adults, measuring BDD severity, insight, depression, functioning and quality of life.[5] A separate analysis examined predictors of response to CBT for BDD,[11] and another proposed empirical definitions of treatment response and remission in BDD.[12]

In adolescents, a follow-up study of 26 participants who had received CBT for BDD examined whether treatment gains were maintained over a longer period,[7] and an earlier case series reported on CBT in adolescents.[10]

The coach-supported app trial was a randomized waitlist-controlled study testing usability and efficacy.[6] A Cochrane review of pharmacotherapy and psychotherapy for BDD also covers the topic.[13] An international expert consensus on BDD treatment, published in 2021, synthesised the evidence for psychological and drug treatments.[14]

Wikipedia reports that people with BDD frequently pursue cosmetic surgery or dermatology and that this typically does not relieve their distress; it recommends that cosmetic surgeons and psychiatrists work together to screen for BDD.[1] Prevalence estimates cited there range from about 2-3 percent in the general population to a higher figure in a global meta-analysis, and about 24 percent among people seeking plastic surgery.[1]

timeline.event: DSM-III-R renames the condition body dysmorphic disorder.[1]
DSM-5 places BDD in the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders group.[1]
Systematic review and meta-analysis of CBT randomized trials for BDD published.[4]
Randomized trial of CBT-BDD versus supportive psychotherapy published in JAMA Psychiatry.[5]
Initial randomized trial of app-based CBT with coach support published.[6]

card.summary: The best-studied talk therapy for body dysmorphic disorder, built around exposure and response prevention.
card.aka: CBT-BDD, exposure and response prevention for BDD
card.note: A clinical treatment for BDD, not a looks-improvement method; see a qualified clinician for diagnosis.

quick.overview:
CBT for BDD is a structured psychotherapy for people who are intensely preoccupied with a perceived flaw in their appearance. It is the best-studied psychological treatment for the condition.

It has been tested in adults, adolescents, and in app-based and digital formats, including a randomized trial against supportive psychotherapy.
quick.mechanism: Sessions typically combine education about BDD, challenging appearance-related beliefs, exposure to feared situations while refraining from rituals such as mirror checking or reassurance seeking, and mindfulness or attention retraining.
quick.risks: Psychotherapy is generally not associated with drug-type side effects, though therapy can be emotionally demanding and access to trained clinicians is limited, which is one reason app-based versions are being studied.
